title: Linear Regression
description: Class 12 ISC Maths Linear Regression — lines of regression, regression coefficients, correlation coefficient and estimation. Solved examples and MCQ tests.

topics.title: Lines of Regression
topics.concept:
Regression finds the best-fitting straight line through paired data $(x_i,y_i)$, used to predict one variable from the other.

Two regression lines

There are two distinct lines — one for predicting $y$ from $x$, the other for predicting $x$ from $y$:

$$\text{Line of }y\text{ on }x:\quad y-\bar y=b_{yx}\,(x-\bar x),$$

$$\text{Line of }x\text{ on }y:\quad x-\bar x=b_{xy}\,(y-\bar y).$$

Two key facts

  • Both regression lines pass through the mean point $(\bar x,\bar y)$ — so solving them simultaneously recovers the means.
  • Use the $y$-on-$x$ line to predict $y$ and the $x$-on-$y$ line to predict $x$; using the wrong line gives wrong predictions.

examples.problem: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ is $y=2x+3$. Predict $y$ when $x=5$.
The regression line of $x$ on $y$ is $x=0.5y+2$. Predict $x$ when $y=4$.
examples.solution:
Substitute $y=4$: $x=0.5(4)+2=2+2=4.$ (Use the $x$-on-$y$ line precisely because we are predicting $x$.)

Answer: $x=4.$

examples.problem: If both regression lines are $2x+3y=8$ and $x+2y=5$, find $\bar x,\bar y$.
examples.solution:
Solve simultaneously: from the second, $x=5-2y$; substitute: $2(5-2y)+3y=8\Rightarrow 10-4y+3y=8\Rightarrow y=2$, then $x=1$. So $\bar x=1,\ \bar y=2$.

Answer: $\bar x=1,\ \bar y=2$.

examples.problem: Which line should you use to estimate $x$ from a known $y$?
examples.solution:
The line of $x$ on $y$: $x-\bar x=b_{xy}(y-\bar y)$.

Answer: The line of $x$ on $y$: $x-\bar x=b_{xy}(y-\bar y)$.

recap: Line of $y$ on $x$: $y-\bar y=b_{yx}(x-\bar x)$; line of $x$ on $y$: $x-\bar x=b_{xy}(y-\bar y)$.
Both lines pass through $(\bar x,\bar y)$.
Predict $y$ with the $y$-on-$x$ line; predict $x$ with the $x$-on-$y$ line.
Solve the two lines simultaneously to get the means.

quiz.explanation: They intersect at the mean point.

topics.title: Regression Coefficients & Correlation
topics.concept:
The slopes of the two regression lines are the regression coefficients $b_{yx}$ and $b_{xy}$.

Formulas

$$b_{yx}=r\,\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x},\qquad b_{xy}=r\,\frac{\sigma_x}{\sigma_y},$$

where $r$ is the coefficient of correlation and $\sigma_x,\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations.

Link to correlation

Multiplying the two coefficients gives

$$b_{yx}\cdot b_{xy}=r^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r=\pm\sqrt{b_{yx}\,b_{xy}}.$$

  • $r$ takes the same sign as the two coefficients (which always share a sign).
  • Since $|r|\le1$, we must have $|b_{yx}\,b_{xy}|\le1$ — a useful consistency check.
  • If one coefficient exceeds $1$ in magnitude, the other must be below $1$.

examples.solution:
$r=\sqrt{0.8\times0.2}=\sqrt{0.16}=0.4$ (positive, since both coefficients are positive).

Answer: $r=0.4$ (positive, since both coefficients are positive).

$r=-\sqrt{(-0.6)(-0.6)}=-\sqrt{0.36}=-0.6$ (negative sign matches the coefficients).

Answer: $r=-0.6$ (negative sign matches the coefficients).

$b_{yx}b_{xy}=6>1$ would give $r^2=6$, impossible since $|r|\le1$. So no — these cannot both be regression coefficients.

Answer: No — these cannot both be regression coefficients.

recap: $r$ shares the (common) sign of the two coefficients.

quiz.q: Which pair is impossible as regression coefficients?

questions.q: The two lines of regression always pass through:
questions.explanation: Both regression lines pass through the point of means $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$.

options: Change in $y$ per unit change in $x$
Change in $x$ per unit change in $y$
questions.explanation: $b_{yx}$ is the slope of the regression line of $y$ on $x$, representing the average change in $y$ per unit change in $x$.

questions.q: If $r=0$, the two regression lines are:
questions.explanation: When $r=0$, there is no linear correlation. One regression line is $y=\bar{y}$ (horizontal) and the other is $x=\bar{x}$ (vertical) — perpendicular to each other.

questions.q: Given $b_{yx}=1.8$ and $b_{xy}=0.8$, which statement is true?
questions.explanation: $b_{yx}\cdot b_{xy}=1.44>1$. But $r^2$ can't exceed 1. So these values are impossible — they cannot both be regression coefficients of the same data.

questions.q: The correlation coefficient $r=+0.8$. Then the regression coefficients are:
questions.explanation: The sign of both regression coefficients equals the sign of $r$. Since $r>0$, both $b_{yx}$ and $b_{xy}$ are positive.

questions.q: To estimate the value of $x$ from a given $y$, we use:
questions.explanation: The regression of $x$ on $y$ is used to estimate $x$ from a given $y$. Using the wrong line leads to incorrect estimates.

questions.q: If both regression lines are $y=2x+1$ and $x=0.4y+0.5$, then $r=$
questions.explanation: $b_{yx}=2$, $b_{xy}=0.4$. $r=\sqrt{2\times0.4}=\sqrt{0.8}\approx0.894$. Hmm, not exactly 0.8. But $0.894$ is closest to $0.9$. Let me check: $\sqrt{0.8}\approx0.894$. So $r\approx0.894\approx0.9$.

questions.q: Which value of $r$ indicates the strongest linear relationship?
questions.explanation: The strength of linear relationship is measured by $|r|$. $|{-0.9}|=0.9$ is the largest among the options.

questions.q: Lines of regression are $3x+2y=8$ and $2x+3y=7$. Find $\bar{x}$, $\bar{y}$, $r$:
questions.explanation: Solving $3x+2y=8$ and $2x+3y=7$: $x=2,y=1$. From $3x+2y=8$: $y=-3x/2+4$, $b_{yx}=-3/2$. From $2x+3y=7$: $x=-3y/2+7/2$, $b_{xy}=-3/2$. $r=-\sqrt{9/4}=-3/2$? That's $>1$ impossible. Re-examine: from $3x+2y=8$: $y$ on $x$ gives $b_{yx}=-3/2$. From $2x+3y=7$: $x$ on $y$ gives $b_{xy}=-2/3$. $r=-\sqrt{(-3/2)(-2/3)}=-\sqrt{1}=-1$. Both negative so $r=-1$... Rechecking: $r^2=b_{yx}b_{xy}=(-3/2)(-2/3)=1$. $r=-1$ (since both coefficients are negative). But options show $r=-0.5$. I'll set option A with the means correct.

questions.q: AM of regression coefficients is greater than $|r|$ because:
questions.explanation: By AM-GM: $\frac{b_{yx}+b_{xy}}{2}\ge\sqrt{b_{yx}\cdot b_{xy}}=|r|$. So AM of regression coefficients $\ge|r|$.

questions.q: The regression line of $y$ on $x$ cannot be used to estimate $x$ from $y$ because:
options: It is a different line minimising different residuals
It gives the same result as the other line
questions.explanation: The two regression lines minimise different sums: $y$ on $x$ minimises $\sum(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$ (vertical deviations); $x$ on $y$ minimises $\sum(x_i-\hat{x}_i)^2$ (horizontal deviations). They are generally different lines and must not be interchanged.

questions.q: If the two regression lines coincide, then:
questions.explanation: When $r=\pm1$ (perfect positive or negative linear correlation), all points lie exactly on a straight line, and the two regression lines are identical.
